blocks.text: Imagine two 15-year-olds in Asia today. One grows in an ecosystem that trains critical reading, nailing, controlling science, and familiar with technology.

Others pass from the system, not yet the ecosystem, who are still struggling to ensure read, count, and think basic. Five or ten years from now, they both go into the same global work market, but with very different foods.
That's where the future of the nation is at stake: the quality of the human being he brought to the field of competition.

The world doesn't wait for Indonesia. Global economy is more appreciative of knowledge, technology, and the ability to rise in class. Other countries are racing to strengthen the human quality, industrial bases, research and innovation. In a competition like this, an unprepared country may grow up, but it is left behind; it is still moving, but it is only a second-tier or third.

For Indonesia, this issue is increasingly urgent because we are entering the demographic bonus window. In the next five to ten years, a huge wave of productive age will either determine whether Indonesia is able to jump or it's trapped. The thing is, Indonesia is not ready.
That unprepared is not present in one form. It appears in five major interconnected weaknesses and, if you don't take it seriously, it will very much determine the fate of Indonesia ahead.

It was born not from opinion or theory alone, but from more than thirty years of research, analysis, observation, and direct experience across the ages, cross-context, and across reality global and domestic history.

Concretively, it covers two worlds at once: the world's advanced power because human capital, research, innovation and technology, and Indonesia themselves in harsh reality, from village to city, from East to West.

Therefore, what is filed here is not a complaint, but a diagnosis of the reality of Indonesia in comparison to the world. In the medical world, misdiagnosis can be expensive. The drugs can be wrong, the action can be wrong, and the result is not healing, it's delaying or even worsening the disease.

The country works with a logic that's not much different. Public policy built on a misleading diagnosis often seems busy, but ineffective; bustling; but shallow; expensive, but doesn't change direction. Therefore, the most important question is not just what to do, but first what is the primary disease.
First of the first big problems.

If we want to understand why Indonesia is still choked up, we have to start from scratch. In development, the foundation is not a complement. He's determined. The fragile base may still be able to support one-two floors, but it will never be strong enough to hold the high buildings. Sooner or later, the crack will be all over the building.
And that's our first problem: the weakness of literacy, numeration and STEM as the foundation of progress.

It's not a small problem. This isn't just some school technical thing. It's an old, chronic, and too long considered ordinary. Yet no nation can advance if too many children are unable to read well, calculate firmly, nakalis critical, and understand science rather well.
The facts are devastating. The PISA 2022 shows this crisis in two layers at once: not only are our foundations fragile, our peaks almost empty.
The proportion of students reaching minimum threshold (Level 2 +; Maximum 6)

Indonesia 18% 25% 34%

At the very least, Indonesia is already behind us. In three fields at once, it's about 50 to 60 percent of Korea, Japan and Singapore. So our problem is not just yet superior. The basic competence limit is still very much achieved on a large scale.

Indonesian 0 * 0 * 0 *
Korean 23% 6% 11%

(0 * means almost zero)

In a superior layer, the image is even louder. Almost no Indonesian students have reached level 5 up in math, reading, or science. It's obvious: we are not only weak on the minimum foundation of a large scale, but also very poor in superior layers.

The World Bank also records that 53% of Indonesian children at the end of elementary school haven't been able to read and understand simple texts by their age. That is, more than half our children have stumbled upon the entrance to learning. If you're behind in elementary school, the next stage is also no better.

For example, in 2015 OECD did a Survey of Adult Skills in over thirty countries, including Indonesia represented by the responders from Jakarta. The findings are clear: nearly 70% of adults are either level 1 or below in literature. They can read text, but not understand it enough. That's Jakarta. Nationally, it must have been worse.

If this isn't a crisis, then what is it? When the foundation reads weak, all other learning goes astray. When numeration is fragile, the ability to understand the economy, technology and modern work is held together. When science and reason don't grow strong, innovation is slogan.

No nation can rise high above the foundation of a crack. If this foundation continues to be left weak, we will not only fail to pursue the future. We're sending millions of children into the future without enough food.

This picture is summed up in the Indonesian Capital Index Human that's at 0.54. It means that the children born in Indonesia today are expected to reach about 54% of the productivity he should have achieved if he had had a full education and good health. Almost half of his potential was lost before he even actually got into the race.

The facts are nothing new. This has been going on for over two decades. It's chronic. What doesn't exist is a systematic, directional and sustainable solution. We're too busy planning, too busy taking care of the edges, not the fundamental ones, and let the root of the problem remain intact. As a result, the circumstances that should be treated as an emergency are allowed to be chronic.
Without taking this foundation seriously, Indonesia Gold will turn into Indonesian Lim.
This is where we get into the next fundamental problem.

(Elwin Tobing, Economic Professor, the President of INADATA, Irvine, US; Writing Book of The NOW or NEVER EMPs which gives the blueprint the transformative ecosystem of national innovation as an absolute requirement to 2050 Golden Indonesia.
